---
title: Cellular respiration in living cells
lang: en
free: true
---
Cellular respiration is the process by which living cells break down glucose and oxygen to release usable chemical energy stored as ATP (adenosine triphosphate). It is the primary way animals, plants, fungi, and most bacteria meet their energy demands. In a sense it is the metabolic reverse of photosynthesis: where photosynthesis builds sugar from carbon dioxide, respiration dismantles sugar back into carbon dioxide and water.

## Glycolysis and the Krebs cycle
Respiration begins in the cytoplasm with glycolysis, splitting one glucose molecule into two pyruvate molecules and yielding a small net gain of ATP. Pyruvate then enters the mitochondria, where it is converted to acetyl-CoA and fed into the Krebs cycle. Each turn of the cycle strips electrons from carbon compounds, passing them to carrier molecules NADH and FADH2 and releasing carbon dioxide as a by-product.

## The electron transport chain
Carrier molecules deliver their electrons to the inner mitochondrial membrane, where a chain of protein complexes passes them along, pumping hydrogen ions across the membrane. The resulting electrochemical gradient drives ATP synthase to produce the bulk of the cell's ATP. Oxygen acts as the final electron acceptor, combining with hydrogen to form water. A single glucose molecule can yield roughly 30–32 ATP molecules through this entire pathway.
